newsitem.title: UK: British financial watchdog warns senior executives.
newsitem.headline: British financial watchdog warns senior executives.

text.p: Sir Andrew Large, the head of Britain's top financial watchdog, on Monday threw his weight behind calls to make senior executives of firms more accountable.

Large, chairman of the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), said individuals at the top of a firm "must take responsibility for ensuring appropriate controls are in place and be prepared to face the consequences if they are not".

In a speech to the Cardiff Business Club in Wales he said the SIB would shortly publish a discussion paper seeking industry's views on this and on proposals to lighten the regulatory touch for firms which proved they were acting responsibly.

"The better you are the less we will do to you," Large said. Firms should decide what risks it would be responsible for them to take, but the regulator will assess how risky they are and how well they control all the risks of their businesses.

Large said such risks encompassed factors such as a firm's corporate and legal structure, the type of business it does, the customers with whom it deals, how it finances itself, its management structure, its remuneration policy or its computer systems.
Once a regulator has completed "a comprehensive risk assessment", then it will have to come up with "the appropriate regulatory response", he added.
While this would give firms an incentive to do better, regulators would, in some cases, need to take disciplinary action against the firm and its senior management if the incentives failed to work.

He said incentives available to regulators were low capital requirements, adjustments in the frequency of regulatory visits or reporting, freedom to take on new business or perhaps a fee structure reflecting a firm's perceived riskiness and the resulting level of regulatory effort.

Large likened the approach, which differed from the tradition of writing rules and making sure that they are not broken, to that recently proposed by the Bank of England for supervising banking institutions.

Large also commented on the recent debate about the level of bonuses being paid in the financial services sector. Some firms had the cultural strength to be able to live with performance related bonus structures "and to be quite confident that these will neither corrupt the controls, nor lead to undue risk taking", he said.

But others cannot. High-profile scandals at Britain's Barings bank, U.S. investment house Kidder Peabody and Japanese bank Daiwa all demonstrated "what can go wrong when there is a mismatch between the perceived expertise of an individual, level of knowledge in the senior management of the firm and the ability...for the controls put in place to cope".

Large pointed out that as firms are given new freedoms and scramble to be first into new areas of financial services, the use of newly developed technologies and information technology can be highly leveraged, as can the risks of getting it wrong.

Where incentives fail, Large said regulators had to be able to call senior managers to account "where the controls and systems they are responsible for implementing and maintaining are inadequate or fail, and where investors can lose out". The key to this was to make senior management's duties more explicit, making it easier to establish "where responsibility lies when major failures occur", Large said.

SIB's discussion paper will outline "various legal issues concerning management responsibility and some preliminary thoughts" including the idea that regulators should develop a code of practice "in the form of principles of good management".

Large said one example could be where a manager delegated any part of his responsibility, he would remain under obligation to ensure he was made aware of anything psing a material risk to the proper discharging of that responsibility.

Another option might be to make firms provide details of their board structure, reporting lines and delegation of responsibilities, including who would be the "primary candidates for discipline in the event of a failure of controls".
The balance between principles and prescription, with the possibility of a move away from detailed rules towards reliance on principles would also be looked at, Large said.
